text: CRISPR-Cas9 was adapted for gene editing by Jennifer Doudna at UC Berkeley and Emmanuelle Charpentier at Umeå University, work that earned them the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, led by Feng Zhang, also developed CRISPR editing tools and secured key patents, leading to a protracted patent dispute between Berkeley and Broad. Editas Medicine, a company co-founded by Zhang, applied CRISPR to treating genetic disorders including sickle cell disease. In 2023, the FDA approved Casgevy, a CRISPR-based therapy developed by Vertex Pharmaceuticals and CRISPR Therapeutics, making it the first approved gene-editing treatment. The European Medicines Agency followed with its own approval in 2024. Ethicists continue to debate germline editing after He Jiankui was sentenced to prison in China for creating CRISPR-edited babies in 2018.
